The Glossy swiftlet (Collocalia esculenta) exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of small, tropical insectivores. Neonates emerge from the egg at a remarkably low mass of approximately 1.18 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.18 grams], a value consistent with the minuscule hatchling sizes observed across the genus and reflecting the altricial developmental mode of swifts. The incubation period itself proceeds at an average nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under these conditions hatching occurs after about 21.5 days [ab = about 21.5 days], a duration that falls within the 19 to 24 day range reported for the species. Growth during the nestling phase is rapid but resource-intensive, with chicks dependent entirely on parental provisioning of aerial arthropods. Once the young bird has completed feather development and achieved the necessary wing loading for sustained flight, fledging takes place at approximately 42 days after hatching [tx = approximately 42 days after hatching], a developmental milestone reached when ambient conditions align with the species' thermal optimum of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].

This modest body size is accompanied by a high mass-specific metabolic rate, which in turn imposes constraints on the energy available for reproduction. The interval between hatching and the first breeding effort is consequently shaped by both physiological preparation and ecological conditions such as prey abundance and nest site availability, particularly for a species that nests colonially in caves and beneath overhangs.

This age at first reproduction reflects the time required to acquire sufficient foraging proficiency and to secure a nesting territory within the colony, a process that may be further protracted in years of poor food availability. This remarkable lifespan, exceeding that of many passerine birds of similar or larger body mass, is likely linked to the species' low extrinsic mortality rate associated with aerial foraging in predator-sparse environments. The extended adult stage allows for repeated reproductive attempts across multiple seasons, partially offsetting the low annual fecundity. Reproductive senescence has not been well documented in this species, but the capacity for breeding appears to be maintained well into advanced age, with the oldest documented individuals still actively provisioning nestlings. This growth trajectory is steeper than that of temperate-zone swifts, likely reflecting the more constant and elevated insect availability in tropical environments.
